content: 1. Records and Population Estimates: Data from medical records are combined with the best estimates for populations lacking viral load data to provide a comprehensive understanding of hepatitis management. 2. Disaggregation of Data: Data is categorized by age, sex, HIV status, geographical location, high-risk populations, and type of medication (e.g., interferon or direct-acting antiviral drugs). 3. Global Reporting Platforms: The WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System is used to validate progress toward hepatitis C elimination and the path to its eradication. 4. Indicator A8 Proportion of People with Chronic Hepatitis B Achieving Viral Suppression: It reflects clinical outcomes and adherence to antiviral therapy. Viral suppression is considered the expected outcome of hepatitis B treatment programs. It is recommended to include information on whether viral load testing is performed universally or selectively and to report the proportion of testing coverage. 5. Global Targets for Hepatitis B: There are no specific global targets for this indicator. The numerator is the number of people with chronic hepatitis B on treatment for at least one year who have achieved viral suppression, while the denominator is the total number of people with chronic hepatitis B on treatment for at least one year and assessed for viral load in the past 12 months. Routine viral load testing is recommended one year after treatment initiation, with more frequent monitoring (every 3–6 months) for individuals with advanced disease, adherence concerns, pregnancy, or renal impairment. 6. Indicator C9a Incidence of HBV Infection in Children Under Five: The goal is to track reductions in chronic hepatitis B, as most of the disease burden arises from infections acquired before the age of five. Prevention efforts focus on this age group. The United Nations has selected the cumulative incidence of chronic hepatitis B at five years of age as an indicator for the Sustainable Development Goal to combat hepatitis. 7. HBsAg prevalence surveys among children under five are used, with sampling designed to be geographically representative. Blood specimens for laboratory testing are preferred for accuracy, though rapid tests may be used in resource-limited settings. 8. Indicator C9b Incidence of Hepatitis C: It tracks progress toward reducing new HCV infections and achieving global hepatitis C elimination targets by 2030. Prevention strategies, including safe medical practices, harm reduction for drug users, and access to testing and curative treatments, are critical to reducing hepatitis C incidence. 9. Global Targets for Hepatitis C: The targets are ≤5 new annual HCV infections per 100,000 population and ≤2 new annual HCV infections per 100 people who inject drugs. 10. Indicator A9 Mother-to-Child Transmission Rate of HBV: It evaluates the impact of interventions to reduce vertical transmission. The global target is a transmission rate of ≤2% in settings using timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccines. 11. Indicator C10 Deaths from HCC, Cirrhosis, and Chronic Liver Diseases Attributable to Hepatitis B and C: This tracks trends in deaths from liver diseases among people with chronic hepatitis B and C. It reflects the ultimate outcomes of prevention, testing, care, and treatment efforts. Improved vital registration and cancer registry coverage will enhance the accuracy of this indicator. The global target is a combined hepatitis Band C-related mortality rate of ≤6 per 100,000 population per year. 12. The fraction of liver disease deaths attributable to hepatitis B and C is estimated using medical records and national mortality data. Alternate data sources include national vital registries, cancer registries, and global disease burden estimates. 13. Disaggregation and Reporting: Data for all indicators are disaggregated by age, sex, HIV status, geographical location, and high-risk populations. Global reporting platforms include the WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System and validation processes for hepatitis elimination.
